title: Towards standardization in soundscape preference assessment
central_proposition: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for standardizing soundscape assessment by defining key concepts, identifying influential contextual factors and desired outcomes, and presenting a universal taxonomy for sound sources, drawing lessons from environmental noise research.

concept_definitions.name: soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: The acoustic environment as perceived and understood by humans, existing through human perception of the acoustic environment of a place.

concept_definitions.name: acoustic environment
concept_definitions.definition: The physical environment of sound, encompassing all waveforms and sound variations in space and time, which is the entity under study in soundscape research.

concept_definitions.name: soundscape quality
concept_definitions.definition: A desired outcome of soundscape assessment, often related to human preference or acoustic comfort.

concept_definitions.name: human preference
concept_definitions.definition: The desired outcome of an individual or group with respect to the acoustic environment, which can be multidimensional and vary by place and context.

concept_definitions.name: direct outcomes
concept_definitions.definition: Outcomes of soundscape assessment where people are consciously aware of sounds and attribute a particular outcome directly to the soundscape (e.g., perceived peacefulness).

concept_definitions.name: enabled outcomes
concept_definitions.definition: Outcomes or activities facilitated by the soundscape without people consciously dissecting why the environment provides well for that activity (e.g., a place being good for relaxation).

concept_definitions.name: context
concept_definitions.definition: Influential factors in soundscape assessment including place/location, physical environment dimensions, personal activity, social environment dimensions, and personal dimensions (e.g., chronic exposure, expectations).

argument_structure: The paper first establishes the need for standardization in soundscape assessment due to diverse approaches and terminology. It then defines soundscape as the human perception of the acoustic environment, distinguishing it from the physical acoustic environment. It argues that soundscape preference is critically dependent on context (place, physical, social, personal dimensions) and the specific outcomes of interest (direct vs. enabled). Finally, it proposes a universal, value-neutral taxonomy of sound sources to facilitate objective reporting and comparability across studies, contrasting soundscape assessment with noise annoyance measurement.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that human perception and evaluation of the acoustic environment, filtered through individual and cultural priors, motivations, and the specific context of a place, construct a 'soundscape' which then elicits a 'preference' or 'quality' judgment. Standardization aims to make the inputs (acoustic environment, context) and outputs (preference, quality) consistently measurable and comparable, allowing for better understanding of the underlying perceptual and cognitive mechanisms. The proposed taxonomy for sound sources aims to standardize the description of the acoustic input, while the discussion of context and outcomes aims to standardize the description of the modulating factors and desired effects.

findings.mechanism: Human perceptual and cognitive processes transform the physical acoustic environment into a subjective soundscape, which is central to the soundscape concept.
findings.quote: Thus a soundscape exists through human perception of the acoustic environment of a place.

findings.mechanism: The specific goals, activities, and cultural expectations associated with a place and context shape what qualities (e.g., peacefulness, liveliness, safety) are preferred in its soundscape.
findings.quote: In different places and in different contexts, a person's preferred outcome with respect to the acoustic environment may differ markedly.

findings.mechanism: Soundscapes can facilitate activities and outcomes either directly (through conscious awareness and attribution) or indirectly/implicitly (by providing an environment conducive to the activity without explicit conscious processing of the soundscape itself).
findings.quote: Assessment of soundscapes should recognize the existence of both direct outcomes (outcomes provided directly by the soundscape) and enabled outcomes (outcomes that are enabled or facilitated by the soundscape).

findings.antecedent: context (place/location, physical environment, personal activity, social environment, personal dimensions, potential users)
findings.mechanism: Contextual factors (e.g., personal history, social norms, physical conditions) shape individual and group expectations, motivations, and experiences, thereby influencing how a soundscape is perceived and preferred.
findings.quote: The discussion so far has emphasized that soundscape preference depends critically on context.

findings.antecedent: universal, value-neutral taxonomy of sound sources
findings.mechanism: A standardized classification system for sound sources provides a common language and framework for objective reporting, reducing ambiguity and improving comparability of findings across different studies and places.
findings.quote: As a basis for standardization in source reporting, we put forward a classification for all sound sources in any acoustic environment-a common framework, or checklist, for broad identification of sources.

findings.mechanism: Soundscape preference assessment is inherently more complex than noise annoyance measurement because it involves multiple, often multidimensional, outcomes, diverse places, and varied human activities, rather than a single, primarily negative outcome.
findings.source: Section 5. Lessons from questionnaire measurement of soundscape
findings.quote: The real distinction between the two fields is in the nature of the outcomes of interest, as will be discussed in Section 4.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: An adequate term for the entity on which soundscape studies focus is the acoustic environment (or less preferably sonic environment) of any place.

A soundscape exists through human perception of the acoustic environment, but it is appropriate to utilize the term soundscape of a place to represent both 'the acoustic environment as perceived by humans' as well as 'the total collection of sounds' of a place, with the latter use restricted to identification or measurement of those sounds by the ear to avoid devaluation and misuse.
People's preferred outcome with respect to the acoustic environment of a place might be varied in different places and contexts.
Standardization of soundscape assessment approaches should accommodate the full range of outcomes or clarify which approaches are appropriate for certain outcomes or places.
Preference is determined in different places and contexts.
There is a need to identify, analyze, and categorize contextual elements for soundscape studies and specify minimum requirements for their reporting.
A generic classification of sound sources, independent of place and free of value judgments, will assist researchers in comparing sound sources across different acoustic environments and studies.
bridge_warrants: The paper draws an analogy between soundscape as the auditory equivalent to visual landscape, recognizing that acoustic and visual components interact in human perception.

The paper contrasts soundscape assessment with environmental noise annoyance studies, highlighting that the key distinction lies in the nature of the outcomes of interest, rather than merely the perceptual basis.
methodological_critiques: The paper critiques the growing and uninformed use of 'soundscape' as a synonym for 'community noise', leading to devaluation and misuse of the term.

It identifies a methodological problem in soundscape assessment where questionnaire methods for preference measurement can introduce an 'experimenter effect' by drawing conscious attention to soundscape elements that might otherwise be implicitly experienced.
It notes that labels, descriptors, and values for sound sources have not been applied uniformly across different acoustic environments in existing soundscape work, hindering comparability.
model_structure: The paper proposes a taxonomy of the acoustic environment (Fig. 1) structured hierarchically. It first categorizes 'places' into Indoor and Outdoor Acoustic Environments (with Outdoor further divided into Urban, Rural, Wilderness, and Underwater). Within these places, it categorizes 'sound sources' into 'Sounds generated by human activity/facility' and 'Sounds not generated by human activity'. Each of these main categories is further subdivided into specific types of sources (e.g., 'Motorised transport', 'Nature') and then into individual sound sources (e.g., 'roadway traffic', 'wildlife'). This taxonomy is designed to be universal, value-neutral, and applicable across all acoustic environments for objective reporting.
limitations: The paper acknowledges that the proposed list of outcomes (Table 1) is illustrative rather than comprehensive, requiring further work on identification, typology, intercorrelations, and association with places/contexts.
It notes that the distinction between direct and enabled outcomes in soundscape assessment requires further study, potentially using methodologies beyond questionnaires (e.g., behavioral studies).
It highlights that further analysis and identification of influential contexts, along with specification of minimum reporting requirements, are needed for standardization.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: A standardized framework is necessary for consistent and comparable assessment of soundscape preferences, linking acoustic environments to human perception and evaluation.

mechanism_chain.description: Conceptual mechanism linking the physical acoustic environment to human soundscape preference, as proposed for a standardized assessment framework.

steps.from_construct: physical acoustic environment (e.g., sound sources, levels, spectral content)

steps.to_construct: cognitive and affective appraisal (e.g., pleasantness, eventfulness, appropriateness, meaning)

instruments_used.name: Sound Level Meters
instruments_used.construct: objective acoustic parameters (e.g., LAeq, Lden, spectral content, specific sound event levels)
instruments_used.description: Devices for measuring physical sound pressure levels and other acoustic metrics in an environment, providing objective data on the acoustic environment.

instruments_used.name: Soundscape Questionnaires
instruments_used.construct: perceived soundscape attributes (e.g., pleasantness, eventfulness, vibrancy, appropriateness), overall preference, emotional responses
instruments_used.description: Self-report instruments designed to capture subjective human perception and evaluation of soundscapes, often using semantic differential scales or rating scales.

instruments_used.name: Acoustic Event Logging/Categorization
instruments_used.construct: identification and quantification of specific sound sources (e.g., birdsong, traffic noise, human voices, music)
instruments_used.description: Methods for systematically identifying, categorizing, and quantifying individual sound events contributing to the overall soundscape, often through observation or audio analysis.
